claim: The adult mouse prostate can be separated into anterior (AP), dorsal (DP), lateral (LP), and ventral (VP) lobes.
source: The mouse prostate can be separated into anterior (AP), dorsal (DP), lateral (LP), and ventral (VP) lobes; the mouse dorsal and lateral lobes are often combined as the dorsolateral prostate (DLP) (Cunha et al., 1987; Shappell et al., 2004; Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cunha et al., 1987; Shappell et al., 2004; Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010).

claim: The mouse dorsal and lateral lobes are often combined as the dorsolateral prostate (DLP).
source: The mouse prostate can be separated into anterior (AP), dorsal (DP), lateral (LP), and ventral (VP) lobes; the mouse dorsal and lateral lobes are often combined as the dorsolateral prostate (DLP) (Cunha et al., 1987; Shappell et al., 2004; Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cunha et al., 1987; Shappell et al., 2004; Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010).

claim: The human prostate lacks defined lobes and is divided into different histological zones (central, transition, and peripheral).
source: In contrast, the human prostate lacks defined lobes, and instead is divided into different histological zones (central, transition, and peripheral); the peripheral zone represents the predominant site of prostate adenocarcinoma, whereas benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) occurs in the transition zone (Cunha et al., 2018; Ittmann, 2018; Shappell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cunha et al., 2018; Ittmann, 2018; Shappell et al., 2004).

claim: The peripheral zone of the human prostate represents the predominant site of prostate adenocarcinoma.
source: In contrast, the human prostate lacks defined lobes, and instead is divided into different histological zones (central, transition, and peripheral); the peripheral zone represents the predominant site of prostate adenocarcinoma, whereas benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) occurs in the transition zone (Cunha et al., 2018; Ittmann, 2018; Shappell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cunha et al., 2018; Ittmann, 2018; Shappell et al., 2004).

claim: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) occurs in the transition zone of the human prostate.
source: In contrast, the human prostate lacks defined lobes, and instead is divided into different histological zones (central, transition, and peripheral); the peripheral zone represents the predominant site of prostate adenocarcinoma, whereas benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) occurs in the transition zone (Cunha et al., 2018; Ittmann, 2018; Shappell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Cunha et al., 2018; Ittmann, 2018; Shappell et al., 2004).

claim: The human prostate has distinct ductal and acinar regions, unlike the mouse.
source: Moreover, unlike the mouse, the human prostate has distinct ductal and acinar regions.
evidence: This claim is stated as established knowledge based on comparison between mouse and human prostate anatomy.

claim: Microarray gene expression profiling has suggested that the DLP is most similar to the human peripheral zone.
source: Although microarray gene expression profiling has suggested that the DLP is most similar to the human peripheral zone (Berquin et al., 2005), there is no consensus on the relationship between mouse lobes and human zones (Ittmann, 2018; Ittmann et al., 2013; Shappell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Berquin et al., 2005).

claim: There is no consensus on the relationship between mouse lobes and human zones.
source: Although microarray gene expression profiling has suggested that the DLP is most similar to the human peripheral zone (Berquin et al., 2005), there is no consensus on the relationship between mouse lobes and human zones (Ittmann, 2018; Ittmann et al., 2013; Shappell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Ittmann, 2018; Ittmann et al., 2013; Shappell et al., 2004).

claim: The adult prostate epithelium is comprised of luminal, basal, and rare neuroendocrine cells.
source: The adult prostate epithelium is comprised of luminal, basal, and rare neuroendocrine cells (Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010; Toivanen and Shen, 2017), and cellular heterogeneity has been suggested within the luminal (Barros-Silva et al., 2018; Chua et al., 2014; Karthaus et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016) and basal compartments (Goldstein et al., 2008; Lawson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010; Toivanen and Shen, 2017).

claim: Cellular heterogeneity has been suggested within the luminal compartment of the prostate epithelium.
source: The adult prostate epithelium is comprised of luminal, basal, and rare neuroendocrine cells (Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010; Toivanen and Shen, 2017), and cellular heterogeneity has been suggested within the luminal (Barros-Silva et al., 2018; Chua et al., 2014; Karthaus et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016) and basal compartments (Goldstein et al., 2008; Lawson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Barros-Silva et al., 2018; Chua et al., 2014; Karthaus et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016).

claim: Cellular heterogeneity has been suggested within the basal compartment of the prostate epithelium.
source: The adult prostate epithelium is comprised of luminal, basal, and rare neuroendocrine cells (Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010; Toivanen and Shen, 2017), and cellular heterogeneity has been suggested within the luminal (Barros-Silva et al., 2018; Chua et al., 2014; Karthaus et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2014; Kwon et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2016) and basal compartments (Goldstein et al., 2008; Lawson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Goldstein et al., 2008; Lawson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2020).

claim: Lineage-tracing analyses have shown that the hormonally intact adult prostate epithelium is maintained by unipotent progenitors within the basal and luminal epithelial compartments.
source: Lineage-tracing analyses have shown that the hormonally intact adult prostate epithelium is maintained by unipotent progenitors within the basal and luminal epithelial compartments (Choi et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Choi et al., 2012; Lu et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).

claim: Following tissue dissociation, both basal and luminal cells can act as bipotent progenitors in organoid or tissue reconstitution assays.
source: However, following tissue dissociation, both basal and luminal cells can act as bipotent progenitors in organoid or tissue reconstitution assays (Chua et al., 2014; Karthaus et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Chua et al., 2014; Karthaus et al., 2014).

claim: The progenitor properties of basal cells may reflect their ability to generate luminal progeny during tissue repair after wounding or inflammation.
source: The progenitor properties of basal cells may reflect their ability to generate luminal progeny during tissue repair after wounding or inflammation (Kwon et al., 2014; Toivanen et al., 2016), but the role of presumptive luminal progenitors has been less clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Kwon et al., 2014; Toivanen et al., 2016) and involves speculative reasoning about the biological role of basal cells.

claim: Several studies have suggested increased progenitor potential in the proximal region of the prostate (nearest to the urethra).
source: In particular, several studies have suggested increased progenitor potential in the proximal region of the prostate (nearest to the urethra) (Burger et al., 2005; Goto et al., 2006; Tsujimura et al., 2002), particularly for proximal luminal cells (Guo et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Burger et al., 2005; Goto et al., 2006; Tsujimura et al., 2002).

claim: Increased progenitor potential has been suggested particularly for proximal luminal cells.
source: In particular, several studies have suggested increased progenitor potential in the proximal region of the prostate (nearest to the urethra) (Burger et al., 2005; Goto et al., 2006; Tsujimura et al., 2002), particularly for proximal luminal cells (Guo et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Guo et al., 2020; Karthaus et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).

claim: Single-cell RNA-sequencing was performed on whole prostates from adult wild-type mice at 10 weeks of age.
source: To examine cellular heterogeneity, we performed single-cell RNA-sequencing of whole prostates from adult wild-type mice at 10 weeks of age.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The full proximal-distal extent of each prostate lobe was microdissected down to its junction with the urethral epithelium.
source: We microdissected the full proximal-distal extent of each prostate lobe down to its junction with the urethral epithelium (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach and references supporting figures.

claim: The anterior (AP), dorsal (DP), and lateral (LP) lobes joined the urethra in close proximity on the dorsal side.
source: We noted that the anterior (AP), dorsal (DP), and lateral (LP) lobes joined the urethra in close proximity on the dorsal side, whereas the ventral lobe (VP) had a distinct junction ventrally.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the study's anatomical analyses.

claim: The ventral lobe (VP) had a distinct junction ventrally with the urethra.
source: We noted that the anterior (AP), dorsal (DP), and lateral (LP) lobes joined the urethra in close proximity on the dorsal side, whereas the ventral lobe (VP) had a distinct junction ventrally.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the study's anatomical analyses.

claim: Each prostate lobe has a characteristic morphology, pattern of ductal branching, and histological appearance.
source: As previously described (Cunha et al., 1987; Shappell et al., 2004; Shen and Abate-Shen, 2010), each lobe has a characteristic morphology, pattern of ductal branching, and histological appearance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and references to figures in the manuscript.

claim: Droplet-based single-cell RNA-sequencing was performed on the 10x Genomics Chromium platform.
source: Droplet-based single-cell RNA-sequencing was performed on the 10x Genomics Chromium platform (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Batch effect correction was performed for aggregation of datasets.
source: For analysis of the resulting data, we performed batch effect correction if needed for aggregation of datasets (Stuart et al., 2019), followed by application of Randomly, an algorithm that uses random matrix theory to reduce noise in single-cell datasets (Aparicio et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim describes the computational methods used and cites the relevant algorithms.

claim: The Randomly algorithm uses random matrix theory to reduce noise in single-cell datasets.
source: For analysis of the resulting data, we performed batch effect correction if needed for aggregation of datasets (Stuart et al., 2019), followed by application of Randomly, an algorithm that uses random matrix theory to reduce noise in single-cell datasets (Aparicio et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the algorithm's publication (Aparicio et al., 2020).

claim: The Randomly algorithm discriminates biological signals from noise and sparsity-induced confounding signals, which typically comprise approximately 98% of the data.
source: Using the universality property of random matrix theory on eigenvalues and eigenvectors of sparse matrices, Randomly discriminates biological signals from noise and sparsity-induced confounding signals, which typically comprise approximately 98% of the data, based on a survey of published single-cell datasets (Aparicio et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the algorithm's publication (Aparicio et al., 2020).

claim: Clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm with selection of the number of clusters based on the mean silhouette score.
source: After de-noising of single-cell data, we performed clustering using the Leiden algorithm as implemented in Wolf et al., 2018, with selection of the number of clusters based on the mean silhouette score.
evidence: This claim describes the computational methods used and cites the relevant algorithm.

claim: Five different luminal epithelial populations were identified in the mouse prostate.
source: Notably, we could identify five different luminal epithelial populations, a single basal population, rare neuroendocrine cells, and a small population of epithelial cells that expresses both basal and luminal markers.
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results presented in the study.

claim: A single basal population was identified in the mouse prostate.
source: Notably, we could identify five different luminal epithelial populations, a single basal population, rare neuroendocrine cells, and a small population of epithelial cells that expresses both basal and luminal markers.
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Rare neuroendocrine cells were identified in the mouse prostate.
source: Notably, we could identify five different luminal epithelial populations, a single basal population, rare neuroendocrine cells, and a small population of epithelial cells that expresses both basal and luminal markers.
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results presented in the study.

claim: A small population of epithelial cells that expresses both basal and luminal markers was identified.
source: Notably, we could identify five different luminal epithelial populations, a single basal population, rare neuroendocrine cells, and a small population of epithelial cells that expresses both basal and luminal markers.
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Distinct stromal and immune components were identified, corresponding to two different stromal subsets and immune cells (macrophages, T cells, B cells).
source: We could also identify distinct stromal and immune components, corresponding to two different stromal subsets (Kwon et al., 2019), as well as immune cells (macrophages, T cells, B cells); some datasets also contained small populations of contaminating vas deferens and seminal vesicle cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results and cites prior work on stromal subsets.

claim: Four of the luminal populations identified in the aggregated dataset were highly lobe-specific.
source: We found that four of the luminal populations identified in the aggregated dataset were highly lobe-specific; hence, we named these populations LumA (AP-specific), LumD (DP-specific), LumL (LP-specific), and LumV (VP-specific).
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis of individual lobes.

claim: LumA is an AP-specific luminal population.
source: We found that four of the luminal populations identified in the aggregated dataset were highly lobe-specific; hence, we named these populations LumA (AP-specific), LumD (DP-specific), LumL (LP-specific), and LumV (VP-specific).
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis of individual lobes.

claim: LumD is a DP-specific luminal population.
source: We found that four of the luminal populations identified in the aggregated dataset were highly lobe-specific; hence, we named these populations LumA (AP-specific), LumD (DP-specific), LumL (LP-specific), and LumV (VP-specific).
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis of individual lobes.

claim: LumL is an LP-specific luminal population.
source: We found that four of the luminal populations identified in the aggregated dataset were highly lobe-specific; hence, we named these populations LumA (AP-specific), LumD (DP-specific), LumL (LP-specific), and LumV (VP-specific).
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis of individual lobes.

claim: LumV is a VP-specific luminal population.
source: We found that four of the luminal populations identified in the aggregated dataset were highly lobe-specific; hence, we named these populations LumA (AP-specific), LumD (DP-specific), LumL (LP-specific), and LumV (VP-specific).
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis of individual lobes.

claim: The LumP population was observed in the datasets for all four lobes and was highly enriched in the proximal portion of each lobe.
source: The remaining luminal population was observed in the datasets for all four lobes and was highly enriched in the proximal portion of each lobe; thus, we termed this population LumP (proximal) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis of individual lobes and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: The LumA and LumD marker Tgm4 was highly expressed by luminal cells in the distal region of the AP and DP.
source: For example, we found that the LumA and LumD marker Tgm4 was highly expressed by luminal cells in the distal region of the AP and DP, and that the LumL marker Msmb marked distal luminal cells in the LP.
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining analyses that validated the single-cell RNA-seq findings.

claim: The LumL marker Msmb marked distal luminal cells in the LP.
source: For example, we found that the LumA and LumD marker Tgm4 was highly expressed by luminal cells in the distal region of the AP and DP, and that the LumL marker Msmb marked distal luminal cells in the LP.
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining analyses that validated the single-cell RNA-seq findings.

claim: The LumP marker Ppp1r1b was highly enriched in luminal cells that were primarily found in the proximal regions of all four lobes.
source: In contrast, the LumP marker Ppp1r1b was highly enriched in luminal cells that were primarily found in the proximal regions of all four lobes (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining analyses that validated the single-cell RNA-seq findings and is illustrated in Figure 1D-F.

claim: More general luminal markers such as androgen receptor (Ar) were expressed in all luminal populations.
source: However, more general luminal markers such as androgen receptor (Ar) were expressed in all luminal populations (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining analyses and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The LumP-containing proximal region extended from inside the rhabdosphincter to the first major ductal branch point in the AP, DP, and VP, but not the LP.
source: We found that the LumP-containing proximal region extended from inside the rhabdosphincter to the first major ductal branch point in the AP, DP, and VP, but not the LP, whereas the bulk of the lobes corresponded to distal regions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on spatial localization analyses and is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: In the AP and DP, there was a discrete boundary in the medial region between the proximal LumP population and distal LumA or LumD populations.
source: In the AP and DP, we found a discrete boundary in the medial region between the proximal LumP population and distal LumA or LumD populations, respectively (Figure 2A,C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analyses and is illustrated in Figure 2A,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The LP had a population between the proximal and distal regions that expressed low levels of LumL markers.
source: In contrast, the LP had a population between the proximal and distal regions that expressed low levels of LumL markers (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analyses and is illustrated in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Distal luminal cells of each lobe had a tall columnar appearance consistent with secretory function.
source: Histological analyses revealed that distal luminal cells of each lobe had a tall columnar appearance consistent with secretory function, whereas proximal LumP cells typically had a cuboidal morphology.
evidence: This claim is based on histological analyses and infers function from morphology.

claim: Proximal LumP cells typically had a cuboidal morphology.
source: Histological analyses revealed that distal luminal cells of each lobe had a tall columnar appearance consistent with secretory function, whereas proximal LumP cells typically had a cuboidal morphology.
evidence: This claim is based on histological analyses.

claim: Rare clusters of 1–10 LumP cells were observed in the distal AP, DP, and LP.
source: Notably, this analysis also revealed heterogeneity in the distal region of each lobe, with rare clusters of 1–10 LumP cells observed in the distal AP, DP, and LP, but more frequent LumP clusters in the distal VP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analyses and is illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: More frequent LumP clusters were observed in the distal VP.
source: Notably, this analysis also revealed heterogeneity in the distal region of each lobe, with rare clusters of 1–10 LumP cells observed in the distal AP, DP, and LP, but more frequent LumP clusters in the distal VP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on histological analyses and is illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: LumA cells displayed dense regions of rough endoplasmic reticulum throughout the cytoplasm, many free ribosomes, and abundant secretory vesicles on the apical surface, typical of secretory cells.
source: LumA cells displayed dense regions of rough endoplasmic reticulum throughout the cytoplasm, many free ribosomes, and abundant secretory vesicles on the apical surface, typical of secretory cells.
evidence: This claim is based on scanning electron microscopy observations.

claim: LumP cells displayed areas of high mitochondrial density, complex membrane interdigitation, and no vesicles.
source: In contrast, LumP cells displayed areas of high mitochondrial density, complex membrane interdigitation, and no vesicles.
evidence: This claim is based on scanning electron microscopy observations.

claim: At the proximal-distal boundary, an abrupt transition between cellular morphologies took place within 1–2 cell diameters.
source: At the proximal-distal boundary, we observed an abrupt transition between cellular morphologies that took place within 1–2 cell diameters.
evidence: This claim is based on scanning electron microscopy observations.

claim: The ultrastructural differences indicate that the LumA and LumP populations represent distinct cell types, rather than cell states.
source: These ultrastructural differences indicate that the LumA and LumP populations represent distinct cell types, rather than cell states.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the ultrastructural observations.

claim: The PrU population was enriched in the most proximal region of all four lobes, residing inside the rhabdosphincter and adjacent to the urethral junction.
source: We found that this small population was enriched in the most proximal region of all four lobes, residing inside the rhabdosphincter and adjacent to the urethral junction (Figure 2D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C); hence, we termed this novel population PrU (periurethral).
evidence: This claim is based on spatial localization analyses and is illustrated in Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The PrU population co-expresses some markers with LumP.
source: Although this PrU population co-expresses some markers with LumP (Figure 1D), it also expresses several urothelial markers such as Ly6d and Aqp3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression analyses and is illustrated in Figure 1D and Figure 2D.

claim: The PrU population expresses several urothelial markers such as Ly6d and Aqp3.
source: Although this PrU population co-expresses some markers with LumP (Figure 1D), it also expresses several urothelial markers such as Ly6d and Aqp3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression analyses and is illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: Nkx3-1 mRNA expression marks epithelial cells in ductal derivatives of the developing urogenital sinus, such as the prostate, but not the urothelium.
source: Consequently, we examined the expression of Nkx3-1, whose mRNA expression marks epithelial cells in ductal derivatives of the developing urogenital sinus, such as the prostate, but not the urothelium (Bhatia-Gaur et al., 1999); similarly, the Nkx3-1Cre driver also marks early prostate bud cells but not the urogenital sinus during development (Thomsen et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Bhatia-Gaur et al., 1999).

claim: The Nkx3-1Cre driver marks early prostate bud cells but not the urogenital sinus during development.
source: Consequently, we examined the expression of Nkx3-1, whose mRNA expression marks epithelial cells in ductal derivatives of the developing urogenital sinus, such as the prostate, but not the urothelium (Bhatia-Gaur et al., 1999); similarly, the Nkx3-1Cre driver also marks early prostate bud cells but not the urogenital sinus during development (Thomsen et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Thomsen et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).

claim: In the adult prostate, Nkx3-1 is expressed by all four distal luminal populations (LumA, LumD, LumL, LumV), but is not expressed by LumP or PrU.
source: In the adult prostate, Nkx3-1 is expressed by all four distal luminal populations (LumA, LumD, LumL, LumV), but is not expressed by LumP or PrU (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression analyses and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The Nkx3-1Cre driver lineage-marks most of the cells in all epithelial populations, including LumP and PrU, but not the urethra.
source: However, we found the Nkx3-1Cre driver lineage-marks most of the cells in all of these populations, including LumP and PrU, but not the urethra (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is based on lineage-tracing experiments and is illustrated in Figure 2E.

claim: The LumP and PrU populations are derived from Nkx3-1 expressing prostate epithelial cells and are distinct from the urothelium.
source: These data indicate that the LumP and PrU populations are derived from Nkx3-1 expressing prostate epithelial cells and are distinct from the urothelium.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the lineage-tracing data.

claim: The distal populations grouped together based on Wasserstein distance analysis, with the LumA and LumD populations being most closely related, followed by LumL and LumV.
source: We found that the distal populations grouped together, with the LumA and LumD populations being most closely related, followed by LumL and LumV.
evidence: This claim is based on computational analysis using optimal transport theory and Wasserstein distance.

claim: The distal populations were next most closely related to LumP, which in turn was most similar to PrU, followed by basal cells.
source: These distal populations were next most closely related to LumP, which in turn was most similar to PrU, followed by basal cells, suggesting a lineage relationship between LumP and distal luminal populations.
evidence: This claim is based on computational analysis using optimal transport theory and Wasserstein distance, and suggests a lineage relationship.

claim: The PrU and basal populations were most efficient at forming organoids, followed by LumP.
source: Despite differences in overall efficiency between media conditions, we consistently found that the PrU and basal populations were most efficient at forming organoids, followed by LumP, whereas the efficiency of distal LumA, LumD, LumL, and LumV was significantly lower (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is based on organoid formation assays and is illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The efficiency of distal LumA, LumD, LumL, and LumV in forming organoids was significantly lower than PrU, basal, and LumP populations.
source: Despite differences in overall efficiency between media conditions, we consistently found that the PrU and basal populations were most efficient at forming organoids, followed by LumP, whereas the efficiency of distal LumA, LumD, LumL, and LumV was significantly lower (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is based on organoid formation assays and is illustrated in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Significant variation in the frequency of graft formation was observed depending on the number and type of input epithelial cells.
source: We observed significant variation in the frequency of graft formation depending on the number and type of input epithelial cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is based on tissue reconstitution assays and is illustrated in Figure 3F.

claim: Each epithelial population typically gave rise to cells of the same type in tissue reconstitution assays, but their ability to generate cells of other populations varied considerably.
source: Based on histological and immunostaining analyses, we found that each epithelial population typically gave rise to cells of the same type, but their ability to generate cells of other populations varied considerably (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on tissue reconstitution assays and is illustrated in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Grafts using distal luminal cells required relatively large numbers of input cells to grow (approximately 30,000 cells).
source: Notably, grafts using distal luminal cells required relatively large numbers of input cells to grow (approximately 30,000 cells) (Figure 3F), and were mostly composed of the same population (i.e. LumA cells generated LumA cells) together with a normal or reduced percentage of basal cells; additionally, these grafts could contain small patches of cells expressing LumP markers on their periphery (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on tissue reconstitution assays and is illustrated in Figure 3F.

claim: LumV cells had the lowest grafting efficiency and generally formed small ductal structures that lacked basal cells.
source: Interestingly, LumV cells had the lowest grafting efficiency and generally formed small ductal structures that lacked basal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on tissue reconstitution assays.

claim: LumP, PrU, and basal cells could produce grafts with significantly lower input cell numbers (approximately 1,000 cells).
source: In contrast, LumP, PrU, and basal cells could produce grafts with significantly lower input cell numbers (approximately 1,000 cells), which contained LumP cells together with multiple distal luminal populations as well as a normal ratio of basal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on tissue reconstitution assays.

claim: Grafts from LumP, PrU, and basal cells contained LumP cells together with multiple distal luminal populations as well as a normal ratio of basal cells.
source: In contrast, LumP, PrU, and basal cells could produce grafts with significantly lower input cell numbers (approximately 1,000 cells), which contained LumP cells together with multiple distal luminal populations as well as a normal ratio of basal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on tissue reconstitution assays.

claim: Both PrU and basal cells possessed high progenitor activity in tissue reconstitution assays, with LumP cells also displaying enhanced activity.
source: Taken together, these results suggest a spectrum of progenitor potential among the different epithelial populations. Both PrU and basal cells possessed high progenitor activity in these assays, with LumP cells also displaying enhanced activity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the organoid and tissue reconstitution assay results.

claim: The distal luminal populations are much less efficient in tissue reconstitution assays compared to PrU, basal, and LumP cells.
source: In contrast, the distal luminal populations are much less efficient in these assays.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the tissue reconstitution assay results.

claim: Two distinct luminal populations were identified in human prostate tissue samples.
source: We identified two distinct luminal populations as well as a PrU-like population (tSNE plots shown in Figure 4A–C; UMAP plots shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and examined their spatial distribution by immunostaining of benign human prostate tissue (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is based on single-cell RNA-seq analysis of human prostate samples and is illustrated in Figure 4A-C.

claim: A PrU-like population was identified in human prostate tissue samples.
source: We identified two distinct luminal populations as well as a PrU-like population (tSNE plots shown in Figure 4A–C; UMAP plots shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and examined their spatial distribution by immunostaining of benign human prostate tissue (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is based on single-cell RNA-seq analysis of human prostate samples and is illustrated in Figure 4A-C.

claim: One human luminal population (Lum Ductal, expressing KRT7 and RARRES1) was primarily localized to ducts.
source: Using specific markers, we found that one luminal population (Lum Ductal, expressing KRT7 and RARRES1) was primarily localized to ducts, whereas the second population was predominantly acinar (Lum Acinar, expressing MSMB and MME), although some intermixing could be observed within ducts (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining analyses of human prostate tissue and is illustrated in Figure 4G.

claim: The second human luminal population was predominantly acinar (Lum Acinar, expressing MSMB and MME).
source: Using specific markers, we found that one luminal population (Lum Ductal, expressing KRT7 and RARRES1) was primarily localized to ducts, whereas the second population was predominantly acinar (Lum Acinar, expressing MSMB and MME), although some intermixing could be observed within ducts (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining analyses of human prostate tissue and is illustrated in Figure 4G.

claim: Some intermixing of Lum Ductal and Lum Acinar populations could be observed within ducts.
source: Using specific markers, we found that one luminal population (Lum Ductal, expressing KRT7 and RARRES1) was primarily localized to ducts, whereas the second population was predominantly acinar (Lum Acinar, expressing MSMB and MME), although some intermixing could be observed within ducts (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining analyses of human prostate tissue and is illustrated in Figure 4G.

claim: The human PrU-like population expressed both basal and luminal genes.
source: As in the mouse, the PrU-like population expressed both basal and luminal genes; similarly, some PrU-like markers were shared with Lum Ductal.
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression analyses of human prostate samples.

claim: Some PrU-like markers were shared with Lum Ductal in human prostate.
source: As in the mouse, the PrU-like population expressed both basal and luminal genes; similarly, some PrU-like markers were shared with Lum Ductal.
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression analyses of human prostate samples.

claim: A PrU-like population is conserved between human and mouse species.
source: This analysis showed that a PrU-like population is conserved between species.
evidence: This claim is based on cross-species comparison using Wasserstein distance analysis.

claim: Human Lum Ductal cells are most closely related to mouse LumP.
source: Furthermore, the human Lum Ductal cells are most closely related to mouse LumP, whereas the Lum Acinar cells are most closely related to LumL followed by LumV.
evidence: This claim is based on cross-species comparison using Wasserstein distance analysis.

claim: Human Lum Acinar cells are most closely related to mouse LumL followed by LumV.
source: Furthermore, the human Lum Ductal cells are most closely related to mouse LumP, whereas the Lum Acinar cells are most closely related to LumL followed by LumV.
evidence: This claim is based on cross-species comparison using Wasserstein distance analysis.

claim: The relationships between human and mouse prostate populations were observed in each of the three human datasets analyzed.
source: Notably, these relationships were observed in each dataset.
evidence: This claim is based on cross-species comparison using Wasserstein distance analysis across multiple datasets.

claim: The ability of LumP and PrU cells to generate luminal distal and basal cells in tissue reconstitution assays suggests that both populations have properties of multipotent progenitors.
source: In tissue reconstitution assays, the ability of LumP and PrU cells to generate luminal distal and basal cells suggests that both populations have properties of multipotent progenitors.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the tissue reconstitution assay results.

claim: Basal cells appear relatively homogeneous, suggesting that previously reported basal heterogeneity may be more limited.
source: In contrast to the luminal compartment, basal cells appear relatively homogeneous, suggesting that previously reported basal heterogeneity (Goldstein et al., 2008; Lawson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2020) may be more limited.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the single-cell RNA-seq analysis results and cites prior literature on basal heterogeneity.

claim: The PrU population is not readily classified in either the basal or luminal compartment as it is comprised of cells with both basal and luminal features.
source: Notably, the PrU population is not readily classified in either compartment as it is comprised of cells with both basal and luminal features.
evidence: This claim is based on the gene expression characteristics of the PrU population.

claim: The LumP population corresponds to the previously reported Sca1high luminal cells.
source: Based on patterns of gene expression, we suggest that the LumP population corresponds to the previously reported Sca1high luminal cells (Kwon et al., 2016) as well as Trop2 (Tacstd2)-positive cells (Crowell et al., 2019), which have been described as proximal progenitor populations with scattered distal cells, and may also be responsible for the enhanced serial grafting efficiency of proximal prostate (Goto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on gene expression patterns and cites prior literature (Kwon et al., 2016).

claim: The LumP population corresponds to Trop2 (Tacstd2)-positive cells.
source: Based on patterns of gene expression, we suggest that the LumP population corresponds to the previously reported Sca1high luminal cells (Kwon et al., 2016) as well as Trop2 (Tacstd2)-positive cells (Crowell et al., 2019), which have been described as proximal progenitor populations with scattered distal cells, and may also be responsible for the enhanced serial grafting efficiency of proximal prostate (Goto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on gene expression patterns and cites prior literature (Crowell et al., 2019).

claim: The LumP population may be responsible for the enhanced serial grafting efficiency of proximal prostate.
source: Based on patterns of gene expression, we suggest that the LumP population corresponds to the previously reported Sca1high luminal cells (Kwon et al., 2016) as well as Trop2 (Tacstd2)-positive cells (Crowell et al., 2019), which have been described as proximal progenitor populations with scattered distal cells, and may also be responsible for the enhanced serial grafting efficiency of proximal prostate (Goto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is speculative and cites prior literature (Goto et al., 2006).

claim: The progenitor activity of LumP and/or PrU-like cells in the human prostate may have been observed by retrospective lineage tracing using mitochondrial mutations.
source: In the human prostate, the progenitor activity of LumP and/or PrU-like cells may have been observed by retrospective lineage tracing using mitochondrial mutations (Moad et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is speculative and cites prior literature (Moad et al., 2017).

claim: The LumP and PrU populations may share some similarities with the 'hillock' and 'club' cells originally described in a cellular atlas of the mouse lung.
source: In addition, the LumP and PrU populations may share some similarities with the 'hillock' and 'club' cells originally described in a cellular atlas of the mouse lung (Montoro et al., 2018) and reported in the human prostate (Henry et al., 2018; Joseph et al., 2020) and in benign human prostate organoids (McCray et al., 2019), but the precise relationship of these populations is unclear.
evidence: This claim is speculative and cites prior literature (Montoro et al., 2018; Henry et al., 2018; Joseph et al., 2020; McCray et al., 2019).

claim: The spatial distribution of LumP and PrU cells may reflect the ability of the prostate to repair itself from a proximal to distal direction in response to extensive tissue damage.
source: Since LumP and PrU cells display multipotent progenitor activity in both organoid formation and tissue reconstitution assays, their spatial distribution may reflect the ability of the prostate to repair itself from a proximal to distal direction in response to extensive tissue damage as well as from distal progenitors in response to more localized injury.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the functional assay results.

claim: The novel PrU population may play a role in prostate tissue repair and/or regeneration.
source: Our findings suggest that the novel PrU population in particular may play a role in prostate tissue repair and/or regeneration, consistent with the previous identification of Ly6d-positive cells as a castration-resistant progenitor (Barros-Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is speculative and cites prior literature (Barros-Silva et al., 2018).

claim: The ability of Nkx3-1Cre to lineage-mark both PrU and LumP, but not the urethra, suggests that these cell populations are distinct from the urothelium.
source: Notably, the ability of Nkx3-1Cre to lineage-mark both PrU and LumP, but not the urethra, suggests that these cell populations are distinct from the urothelium, despite the molecular similarities between the proximal prostate and the urethra noted in a recent report (Joseph et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on lineage-tracing data and cites a recent report (Joseph et al., 2020).

claim: Mouse proximal and distal regions are most related to human ductal and acinar regions, respectively.
source: Specifically, we speculate that mouse proximal and distal regions are most related to human ductal and acinar regions, respectively, and that the mouse LP is most similar to the human peripheral zone.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on the cross-species comparison results.

claim: The mouse LP is most similar to the human peripheral zone.
source: Specifically, we speculate that mouse proximal and distal regions are most related to human ductal and acinar regions, respectively, and that the mouse LP is most similar to the human peripheral zone.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on the cross-species comparison results.

claim: The DP differs significantly from the LP at the anatomical and molecular levels.
source: Few if any studies have specifically assessed tumor phenotypes in the LP, as it is small and usually combined with the DP as the dorsolateral prostate (DLP); however, our analyses show that the DP differs significantly from the LP at the anatomical and molecular levels.
evidence: This claim is based on the anatomical and molecular analyses presented in the study.

claim: A re-evaluation of tumor phenotypes in genetically engineered mouse models may reveal a closer similarity to human prostate tumor histopathology than previously appreciated.
source: Consequently, we suggest that a re-evaluation of tumor phenotypes in genetically engineered mouse models may reveal a closer similarity to human prostate tumor histopathology than previously appreciated.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on the findings about anatomical relationships between mouse and human prostate.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that luminal cells as well as basal cells can serve as the cell of origin for prostate cancer.
source: Previous studies have suggested that luminal cells as well as basal cells can serve as the cell of origin for prostate cancer (Wang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014; Xin, 2019), yet known differences in human prostate cancer outcome (e.g. Zhao et al., 2017) cannot be simply explained on this basis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Wang et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014; Xin, 2019).

claim: Both distal and proximal luminal cells can serve as cells of origin for prostate cancer.
source: Notably, previous studies suggest that both distal and proximal luminal cells can serve as cells of origin for prostate cancer.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior studies.

claim: Prostate tumors arise following deletion of Pten by the Nkx3.1-CreERT2 driver, which is specific for distal luminal cells.
source: For example, prostate tumors arise following deletion of Pten by the Nkx3.1-CreERT2 driver, which is specific for distal luminal cells (Wang et al., 2013), as well as by the Ck4-CreERT2 driver, which is specific for LumP cells (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Wang et al., 2013).

claim: Prostate tumors arise following deletion of Pten by the Ck4-CreERT2 driver, which is specific for LumP cells.
source: For example, prostate tumors arise following deletion of Pten by the Nkx3.1-CreERT2 driver, which is specific for distal luminal cells (Wang et al., 2013), as well as by the Ck4-CreERT2 driver, which is specific for LumP cells (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature (Guo et al., 2020).

claim: An aggregated dataset composed of 5288 cells from two whole prostates was analyzed.
source: We identified distinct luminal, basal, and neuroendocrine populations that were annotated based on the expression of marker genes, as visualized in an aggregated dataset composed of 5288 cells from two whole prostates (tSNE plot shown in Figure 1A,D; UMAP plot shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim describes the dataset analyzed and references the figures.

claim: The Randomly algorithm is based on the three-fold structure of a single-cell dataset: a random matrix (95% or more), a sparsity-induced (fake) signal, and a biological signal.
source: The Randomly algorithm is based on the three-fold structure of a single-cell dataset: a random matrix (95% or more), a sparsity-induced (fake) signal, and a biological signal.
evidence: This claim describes the computational method used in the study.

claim: The algorithm uses the universality properties of random matrix theory for both eigenvalues and eigenvectors to detect the biological signal.
source: The algorithm uses the universality properties of random matrix theory for both eigenvalues and eigenvectors to detect the biological signal.
evidence: This claim describes the computational method used in the study.

claim: Randomly can assist in identification of populations (e.g. PrU) by removing noise and sparsity-induced signals, and by selecting genes responsible for the biological signal.
source: Randomly can assist in identification of populations (e.g. PrU) by removing noise and sparsity-induced signals, and by selecting genes responsible for the biological signal.
evidence: This claim describes the utility of the computational method used in the study.

claim: Two independent biological replicate samples of whole prostate were submitted for scRNA-seq, with 2361 and 2,927 cells sequenced.
source: For the mouse prostate, two independent biological replicate samples of whole prostate were submitted for scRNA-seq, with 2361 and 2,927 cells sequenced.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample sizes.

claim: Two separate biological replicates for individual lobes were used for scRNA-seq, with 1,581–2,735 cells sequenced per sample.
source: Two separate biological replicates for individual lobes were also used for scRNA-seq, with 1,581–2,735 cells sequenced for sample.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample sizes.

claim: Three independent human prostate samples that corresponded to regions of benign histology were submitted for scRNA-seq, with 1,600, 2,303, and 2,825 cells sequenced, respectively.
source: For human prostate (Figure 4—source data 1), three independent samples (#1–3) that corresponded to regions of benign histology were submitted for scRNA-seq, with 1,600, 2,303, and 2,825 cells sequenced, respectively.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental design and sample sizes for human samples.

claim: Single-cell datasets have been deposited in GEO under accession number GSE150692.
source: Single-cell datasets have been deposited in GEO under accession number GSE150692, and can also be accessed through the Broad Institute Single-Cell Portal (www.singlecell.broadinstitute.org).
evidence: This claim provides information about data availability.
